statement: The dot product (or scalar product) is an algebraic operation that takes two equal-length sequences of numbers and returns a single number, defined algebraically as the sum of the products of their corresponding entries: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \sum_{i} a_i b_i = \mathbf{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{b}. In Euclidean geometry, for two Euclidean vectors, it is equivalently defined as the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left\|\mathbf{a}\right\| \left\|\mathbf{b}\right\| \cos \theta.

symbols.meaning: First vector or sequence of numbers
Second vector or sequence of numbers

properties.why: Multiplication of real numbers and vector magnitudes is commutative: \left\|\mathbf{a}\right\|\left\|\mathbf{b}\right\|\cos\theta = \left\|\mathbf{b}\right\|\left\|\mathbf{a}\right\|\cos\theta
The dot product is additive, distributive, and homogeneous under scalar multiplication in both arguments

properties.property: Positive definiteness: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = \left\|\mathbf{a}\right\|^2 \ge 0, with equality if and only if \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}
properties.why: The dot product of a vector with itself equals the square of its Euclidean length

properties.property: Orthogonality: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0 for non-zero vectors if and only if they are orthogonal
properties.why: The angle between orthogonal vectors is \pi/2, where \cos(\pi/2) = 0
The scalar projection of \mathbf{a} along \mathbf{b} is a_b = \left\|\mathbf{a}\right\|\cos\theta = \mathbf{a} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{b}}
The dot product yields a scalar and is not defined between a scalar and a vector

properties.property: No cancellation law: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} with \mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0} does not imply \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{c}
properties.why: \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}) = 0 only requires \mathbf{a} to be perpendicular to (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c})
Holds when \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} are vector-valued differentiable functions

assumptions.assumption: Equal dimension: vectors have the same number of entries
assumptions.breaks_when: Vectors are of unequal lengths, making pairwise products and summation undefined
Working in non-Euclidean geometries or complex vector spaces where conjugate symmetry is required

failure_modes.cause: Attempting to take the dot product of two sequences or vectors of different dimensions
Overlooking that the difference vector \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c} may be non-zero and perpendicular to \mathbf{a}
Treating the dot product as an associative binary operation on vectors, ignoring that the result of the first dot product is a scalar
